case.case_title: Thiranagama v. Madihahewa, Commissioner-General of Labour and Others

clause.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the petitioner, an Inspector of Internal Trade Grade II, was unlawfully denied appointment as a Labour Officer on the basis of irrational and discriminatory criteria violating Article 12(1) of the Constitution.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner argued that despite having equal marks (115) as other candidates who were appointed, and meeting the qualifications stipulated by the recruitment scheme, he was denied appointment due to an irrational interpretation of 'allied grades' that excluded his grade, thus violating his right to equality under Article 12(1).
case_context.respondent_argument: The respondents contended that only Inspectors of Internal Trade Grade I fell within the 'allied grades' eligible for appointment, and that the petitioner, being Grade II, was not eligible under the recruitment scheme and Gazette notifications. They also argued that previous appointments were made under different procedures.
key_facts: Petitioner scored 115 marks in the Limited Competitive Examination but was not appointed.
Candidates with equal or lower marks were appointed.
Petitioner was a confirmed officer with 5 years of service and a recognized university degree.
Respondents relied on a recruitment scheme and Gazette notifications that defined eligibility as being in clerical or 'allied grades', interpreted to exclude Grade II Inspectors.
Sinhala version of the recruitment scheme used the term 'parallel grade' rather than 'allied grade'.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The court interpreted Article 12(1) as guaranteeing equality before the law and equal protection, which was infringed by the irrational and inconsistent application of eligibility criteria. The court emphasized that the Sinhala version of the recruitment scheme referred to 'parallel grades', which included the petitioner’s grade, and that previous appointments of Grade II Inspectors as Labour Officers supported this interpretation.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The court found that excluding the petitioner on the basis that he was not in an 'allied grade' was neither rational nor consistent with the Sinhala version of the scheme or past practice. The petitioner’s qualifications and service met the criteria, and the differential treatment violated his fundamental right to equality.
principles_established: Equality before the law requires rational and consistent application of recruitment criteria.
Discrepancies between language versions of official documents must be considered in interpretation.
Past consistent practice is relevant in interpreting eligibility criteria.
Fundamental rights under Article 12(1) protect against arbitrary discrimination in public employment.

outcome.holding: The court held that the petitioner’s fundamental right under Article 12(1) was violated and ordered his appointment as a Labour Officer with back wages, allowances, compensation, and costs.
outcome.remedy_or_orders: Direct the Public Service Commission and Commissioner-General of Labour to appoint the petitioner as Labour Officer, Grade II, with effect from 26 November 2001, with back wages, allowances, compensation of Rs. 50,000, and costs.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 12(1) was central to the court’s reasoning as it protects equality before the law and equal protection, which was infringed by the discriminatory and irrational exclusion of the petitioner from appointment despite meeting the criteria.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The petitioner scored 115 marks, equal to others appointed, but was excluded on the basis that he was not in an 'allied grade' as per the recruitment scheme. The Sinhala version referred to 'parallel grade' which included him. The court found this exclusion irrational and violative of Article 12(1).
